title: Tier 2 manifest
description: One entry in registry/. Git is the system of record for Tier 2, and a manifest is what git carries in place of the bytes (ADR-0023). It names an object by content digest and says where the bytes actually live, so that a release can be cited, re-acquired and verified without this repository ever holding it.

kind.description: Which registry namespace this entry belongs to; the seven directories under registry/. Closed, because a manifest filed under a namespace nobody reads is indistinguishable from one that was never written.

digest.description: The content address of the manifested object (ADR-0005). This is the identity — the filename, the namespace and the deposition URL are all conveniences that could be wrong; this cannot.

name.description: The mutable name the object is published under — dataset_id, method_id and so on (ADR-0005). Optional, and never an identity: an Evaluation pins the digest above, never this.

version.description: The version label under `name`. Human-facing; the digest is what is pinned.

tier.description: ADR-0023. Tier 0: raw source archives, referenced by descriptor and NEVER stored or redistributed. Tier 1: canonical releases, deposited externally with a DOI. Tier 2: derived artifacts small enough that git is the system of record. The tier decides which of `retrieval`, `deposition` and `path` this manifest must carry, so it cannot be omitted or inferred.

recorded_at.description: When this manifest entry was written. A recorded fact, not an identifier: ADR-0005 forbids timestamp identifiers for immutables, and the digest above is the identity.

class.description: ADR-0023 lifecycle and STD-24. `permanent`: a Tier 1 release, or a Tier 2 artifact referenced by an Evidence Binding. `prunable`: an unreferenced run artifact, eligible for pruning after 90 days. Declared rather than derived, so a retention run reads a decision instead of re-deriving one it could get wrong.

referenced_by.description: Claim identifiers whose Evidence Bindings depend on these bytes. A non-empty list is why `class` is permanent; E6 §11(iv) makes such an artifact never prunable.

prune_after.description: The earliest instant this artifact may be pruned. Present only on a prunable entry, and absent rather than null on a permanent one — a permanent artifact has no such instant, and writing one would invite a reader to believe it does.

retention.description: What may happen to these bytes, and when.

provider.description: The archive holding the bytes, e.g. the ISSDC science archive.

locator.description: What a future reader needs in order to re-acquire this artifact from `provider`. ADR-0023 requires that any stage be able to re-acquire from the descriptor, so this is required rather than advisory.

requires_credentials.description: Whether re-acquisition needs an authenticated session. Recorded because a reader who cannot obtain one needs to know that before trying, not after. The credentials themselves never appear here or anywhere outside Ingest (STD-19).

retrieval.description: How to re-acquire Tier 0 bytes this repository deliberately does not hold (ADR-0023, STD-23).

provider.description: Where the release was deposited — Zenodo, or the repository-release fallback.

url.description: Where the deposited bytes can be fetched. https only: a plaintext locator for an artifact whose whole purpose is verifiable integrity would undermine the claim in transit.

doi.description: The citable identifier, or null where the fallback path was used. Required as a field and nullable in value: ADR-0023 says the fallback degrades citability and that the degradation is published rather than hidden, so absence must be visible rather than expressed by omitting the field.

path.description: Repository-relative path of a Tier 2 payload carried in git. Constrained to reject absolute paths and any `..` segment: a manifest is read by tooling that will open what it names, and a path escaping the repository root is the difference between reading an artifact and reading anything on the machine.

allOf.$comment: Tier 0 is never deposited and never stored (ADR-0023, E6 §11(iii), STD-23). Making `deposition` and `path` structurally impossible here is stronger than a rule someone must remember: a manifest that would redistribute raw source bytes cannot be written.
A Tier 1 release lives at its deposition. It has no retrieval descriptor — that form is for bytes this project does not hold — and it is not in git.
Git is the system of record for Tier 2, so the payload is at a path and nowhere else.

A permanent artifact has no instant after which it may be pruned. Permitting a `prune_after` alongside `permanent` would let a manifest state a contradiction that a retention run would then have to arbitrate (STD-24, E6 §11(iv)).

A prunable artifact must say when, and must be referenced by nothing. E6 §11(iv): an artifact referenced by an Evidence Binding is NEVER pruned, so `prunable` with a non-empty `referenced_by` is the one combination that would let a published claim lose the bytes underneath it.
ADR-0023 lifecycle: Tier 1 is permanent. A prunable Tier 1 release would make a DOI resolve to nothing.
